abstract: Microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) remains broadly refractory to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need for strategies that convert immunologically "cold" tumors into therapy-responsive states. Here, we identify 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), the rate-limiting enzyme in tyrosine catabolism, as a modulator of sorafenib sensitivity in MSS-CRC. Pharmacological inhibition of HPD by the FDA-approved orphan drug nitisinone synergized with sorafenib across patient-derived organoids, human PBMC-tumor co-cultures, and immunocompetent orthotopic models. Mechanistically, nitisinone imposes strict glutaminolysis dependency, whereas sorafenib disrupts cRaf-MEK-ERK signaling to trigger proteasomal cMYC degradation and transcriptional repression of GLS1, thereby ablating compensatory glutamine anaplerosis. This dual metabolic blockade creates a synthetic lethal trap, provoking irreversible mitochondrial collapse and mtDNA release, which activates the cGAS-STING pathway and drives intratumoral infiltration of cytotoxic NK and CD8+ T cells. Critically, ρ⁰ cells and STING-deficient models confirm mitochondrial damage as the "trigger" of cell death and STING as the "amplifier" of antitumor immunity. In TCGA MSS-CRC cohorts, a double-low glutamine/tyrosine metabolic signature was associated with prolonged survival, enhanced cGAS-STING signaling, and immune-hot tumor features, findings corroborated by single-cell RNA-seq analyses. Finally, the triple combination of nitisinone, sorafenib, and anti-PD-1 therapy achieved superior antitumor efficacy with favorable tolerability in vivo. Collectively, our findings delineate a metabolic-mitochondrial-STING axis and support repurposing nitisinone as a promising translational strategy to sensitize MSS-CRC to immunotherapy.
